rationale: Hunter Definition 4.1 defines convergence and the sum through partial sums and notes that changing the starting index does not change convergence. The item adopts the equivalent exclusive-sum convention s_n=sum_{k<n}a_k, includes divergence to both infinities, and formalises arbitrary starting indices, so it is a convention-adapted definition rather than a verbatim copy.

Hunter states that a series may start at any index without changing convergence, and the definition of partial sums yields the sourced finite-prefix principle. The item packages the exact tail identity, sum splitting, and the every-tail/some-tail equivalence in the library's exclusive-sum convention. The numbered derivation is locally expanded.

Hunter Theorem 4.9 states exactly that convergence of a real series forces its terms to tend to zero; its contrapositive is logically identical. The item's arbitrary-starting-index paragraph is only the library's shift convention. The proof follows Hunter's Cauchy-tail argument with local indexing.

Hunter Theorem 4.8 gives the same iff Cauchy block criterion. The item changes from inclusive partial sums indexed from 1 to exclusive partial sums indexed from 0 and writes the block as sum_{k=m+1}^n a_k; these are convention deltas only. Its proof is the sourced partial-sum Cauchy argument adapted to those indices.

Linearity follows from the sourced definition of a series as a limit of partial sums and the standard algebra of limits. The item combines addition, scalar multiplication, and the nonzero-scalar iff/divergence form into one library-facing lemma. The proof is locally composed from finite-sum and limit laws.

Hunter Proposition 4.17 and Semmes Proposition 3.7.13 state exactly that every absolutely convergent real (indeed complex) series converges. The proof follows the standard sourced comparison of each finite tail with the absolute-value tail, expressed through the local Cauchy criterion.

Hunter Example 4.2 gives the exact sum 1/(1-r) for |r|<1 and records divergence for r>=1 and oscillatory divergence for r<=-1, exactly the two regimes in the item. The proof uses the same finite geometric-sum identity and null-power limit with local dependencies made explicit.

Hunter §4.1 states that sum(a_n-a_{n+1}) has partial sums a_1-a_{n+1}; the item gives the identical result from index 0, adds the iff with convergence of b_k, the value of the sum, and the general-start shift. The proof is the standard telescoping calculation adapted to exclusive finite sums.

Hunter Proposition 4.6 states exactly that a nonnegative series converges iff its partial sums are bounded above and otherwise diverges to infinity. The item additionally identifies the sum with the supremum, an immediate monotone-convergence consequence. The proof follows that sourced monotone-partial-sum argument.

Hunter Theorem 4.19 gives the standard comparison theorem, and the item's nonnegative eventual inequality is its positive-series specialization together with the contrapositive divergence form and tail invariance. The proof is the standard bounded-partial-sum comparison adapted to an eventual bound.

The University of North Dakota theorem gives all three regimes: positive finite limit gives common behaviour, zero gives convergence only from the comparison series to the smaller one, and infinity gives divergence only from the comparison series to the larger one. The item uses real convergence versus divergence to +infinity explicitly, adds contrapositives, and shifts from index 1 to 0. Its proof follows the standard eventual two-sided inequalities.

Semmes Theorem 3.9.1 states exactly that a monotonically decreasing nonnegative family from 1 has a convergent series iff its condensed series sum 2^k a_{2^k} converges. The proof follows the sourced dyadic block bounds, with the local finite-sum and index conventions written out.

Hunter Example 4.21 and Semmes's condensation chapter give the standard iff threshold p>1 for positive real exponents. The item restricts to rational p because that is the power operation available at this reading level and formalises canonical naturals, so it is a semantic specialization. The proof is the standard condensation-to-geometric-series argument.

Hunter Theorem 4.27 states the limsup root test with absolute convergence below 1 and divergence above 1; the surrounding text gives both outcomes at equality. The item merely reindexes |a_n|^(1/n) as |a_{k+1}|^(1/(k+1)) to avoid exponent 1/0. Its proof follows the sourced geometric comparison.

The source states the limsup/liminf ratio test exactly: limsup below 1 gives absolute convergence and liminf above 1 gives divergence, with the intervening regime inconclusive. The item makes nonvanishing and the index-shift convention explicit. Its proof is the standard eventual geometric comparison.

The CSUDH notes give the full ratio-root liminf/limsup chain, state that the root test is strictly stronger, and use the same sequence 2^{(-1)^n-n} as witness. The item shifts indices and expands both convergence and divergence translations through local test statements. Its proof follows the sourced inequality-and-witness argument.

Thomson–Bruckner–Bruckner Theorem 3.37 gives exactly the positive-weight Kummer expression, the positive-liminf convergence criterion, and the eventual-nonpositive plus divergent reciprocal-weight criterion. The proof follows the sourced telescoping comparison, expanded with extended-real tail-infimum details.

Both textbooks explicitly identify d'Alembert's ratio test as Kummer's test with constant weights. The item states only the two limsup/liminf ratio conclusions recovered in the positive-term setting and proves them through reciprocal bounds, so it is an expanded semantic specialization.

The sources state Raabe's positive-term test and identify it as Kummer with harmonic weights. The item uses k+1 rather than k because its naturals start at zero, and uses liminf/limsup rather than assuming a single limit. The proof is the sourced Kummer specialization with that convention delta.

The sources state Gauss's test for a_n/a_{n+1}=1+alpha/n+O(n^{-beta}) with beta>1, convergent exactly for alpha>1. The item's bound |r_k|<=C k^{-1-epsilon}, epsilon positive rational, is the same big-O regime after choosing beta=1+epsilon, with local rational-power conventions. Its borderline proof is a locally constructed summable-error product argument rather than the sourced logarithmic/Kummer proof.

The source states the divergent-series Abel–Dini–Pringsheim theorem for positive terms with inclusive partial sums S_n: sum a_n/S_n diverges and sum a_n/S_n^t converges for t>1, hence in particular at t=2. These are exactly the item's two claims and convention. The local proof derives the two estimates directly from Cauchy and telescoping facts.

The source set establishes the ratio-root strength order, Kummer specializations, Raabe and Gauss criteria, and the Abel–Dini no-final-comparison obstruction. The item is a repository-specific synthesis of those results and local availability constraints. It also contains one inaccurate alteration about a 1/(k log k) Gauss remainder, recorded as an A2 falsehood; as a Remark it has no separate proof component.

Hunter places the divergent harmonic series immediately after the nth-term condition precisely to show that terms tending to zero are not sufficient. The item turns that standard failed converse into an explicit false statement and refutes it with the same family under the local index convention. The numbered refutation is locally written.

The sourced ratio test requires liminf>1 for divergence, while the CSUDH notes give oscillating-ratio geometric witnesses showing why limsup cannot replace it. The item formulates the pedagogical false alteration and uses a closely related bounded oscillating multiplier. The detailed computation is local.

The Abel–Dini–Pringsheim theorem explicitly constructs, from any divergent positive series, another divergent positive series with smaller terms; this rules out a slowest divergent series and any single universal comparison series. The item presents the negation as a false claim and follows the sourced construction b_n/B_n with local quantifiers made explicit.

Hunter Example 4.11 states that the harmonic series diverges and gives the same powers-of-two block argument and logarithmic-rate lower bounds. The item adds a condensation proof and formalises the explicit lower bound in local finite-sum notation; its Oresme block proof follows the source. At A8, Alpha replaced an unsourced universal superlative about the slowest explicit divergence on the page with the narrower sourced-compatible description that the lower bound is a quantitative witness to slow divergence; this material repair makes the public Example component ai-altered.

Hunter Example 4.20 proves convergence of sum 1/n^2 by the same comparison 1/(n+1)^2<1/(n(n+1)) and obtains the upper bound 2. The item shifts that calculation to k>=2 and states the safe non-strict bound at most 2. Its verification follows the sourced telescoping comparison.

Hunter gives the geometric sum formula and its starting-index convention. The two values 1 for sum_{k>=1}2^{-k} and 3/4 for sum_{k>=0}(-1/3)^k are direct specializations packaged together by the item. Their local arithmetic verification is not a traced source proof.
Hunter Example 4.5 gives exactly sum_{k>=1}1/(k(k+1))=1 through the identity 1/(k(k+1))=1/k-1/(k+1). The item's verification is the same telescoping calculation with local dependency citations.

The sources apply condensation to the p-series and obtain the geometric ratio 2^{1-p}, with the threshold p>1. The item restricts to rational exponents, displays the algebra separately, and tabulates p=1/2,1,2. Its verification follows the sourced calculation under local rational-power notation.

The Abel–Dini source explicitly applies the theorem to the harmonic series and records the logarithmically corrected family, while Hunter supplies the harmonic divergence. The item uses exact inclusive harmonic sums and selects exponents 1 and 2. The direct dependency application is locally written; its inaccurate 'no last divergent series in the family' sentence is an A2 defect.

The sources state that Raabe decides positive series whose ordinary ratio tends to 1 and give the p-series as the governing family. The item specializes to p=2 and computes R_k=2+1/(k+1) exactly, while the ratio tends to 1. This particular worked verification is locally composed.

The CSUDH notes use the same sequence 2^{(-1)^n-n}, compute alternating ratios 1/8 and 2, and obtain root limit 1/2 to show strict root-test dominance. The item translates that standard witness into the library's alternating-sequence interface and cites the earlier computation; its proof is an adapted sourced verification.

The sources state that the root test is inconclusive at 1 and use p-series on opposite sides of the threshold. The item chooses p=1/2 and p=2, proves both root quantities equal 1 using the local nth-root lemma, and is therefore a worked semantic specialization. The detailed root calculation is local.

The item is the standard direct-comparison theorem with its nonnegativity hypothesis removed, refuted by the negative harmonic series below the zero series. That is a recoverable alteration of the sourced theorem, not a novel mathematical claim. The explicit signed witness and verification are locally chosen.

The item is Cauchy condensation with the sourced monotonicity hypothesis deleted. Its power-of-two zero set is a concrete local witness: the condensed series vanishes while the original terms equal 1 arbitrarily late. The false proposition is a recoverable alteration; the witness proof is local.

The UND statement gives only the direction from convergence of the larger comparison series to convergence of the smaller series when the quotient limit is zero. The item reverses that sourced implication and refutes it with the standard p=2 versus p=1 pair. The indexed verification is locally written.
